editor_spans.body: The most concrete part of the Motherwell speech comes near the end and is easy to miss among the stories about steelworks and football. Burnham offers to devolve DWP employment support, but only if Scotland follows the 'Easterhouse principle' and runs it from the bottom up. Employment support is one of the few levers Westminster still holds over everyday life in Scotland, and here it is attached to a condition about how Holyrood governs. That makes the 'genuine offer' more pointed than his pre-briefing let on. Westminster is offering to hand over a reserved power, and the price is that Edinburgh agrees to push power down to local level as well. If the Scottish Government accepts, it takes on the Prime Minister's model of local delivery. If it refuses, it looks like the government holding on to power. That fits what we said about the pre-briefing: the offer works as a wedge whatever Holyrood answers.

His diagnosis is that Scotland, 'the most devolved nation in the UK, is itself one of the most centralised nations in Europe'. That is broadly fair, but it comes from a long history the speech leaves out. Scotland's councils were reorganised in 1996 into 32 large unitary authorities, which put local government a long way from the communities it serves. From 2007 Holyrood froze council tax for most of a decade and paid councils from the centre to make up the money. That left councils relying on Edinburgh's block grant, which Edinburgh relied on getting from London. So the centralisation he criticises was not an accident of the 1999 settlement. It came from the way money flows: every level of government in Scotland depends for its funding on the level above it. Handing down powers over 'innovation, enterprise and employability' changes little unless the funding and the power to raise money at local level change too. The speech promises the first and says nothing about the second.

The story about the Greater Manchester buses deserves a closer look. In 2025 Alexander Dennis said it might move its Falkirk production to Scarborough because UK orders had dried up and Chinese manufacturers were winning on price. Contracts from a single mayor did not secure its future in Scotland. That is the real test of his 'circular benefits' argument. A procurement rule that only works when one politician decides to pay a bit more cannot rebuild industry. It has to be written into rules every public buyer follows, and it has to fit trade law. He promises this for 'all public procurement in the UK', but gives no mechanism, while the same speech looks forward to closer ties with the EU, whose rules limit buy-local procurement.

Ravenscraig is a good place to make the argument, but it complicates it too. The works closed in 1992, four years after British Steel was privatised. The decision was taken in a company boardroom as well as in Whitehall, and it followed a world steel market that no Scottish region could have resisted on its own. Devolving decisions to communities is not wrong, but local control alone would not have kept Ravenscraig open. The places in this speech, from Motherwell and Leigh to Aberdeen and Grangemouth today, were hollowed out by forces of capital and global trade, not just by distance from London. Moving power down to local level is the part he talks about most. Whether the money and those wider forces will follow is the part he does not answer.
